messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

When I first met Alonzo, he was a 45‑year‑old farmer who had grown up on a small plot of land in the southeastern United States. As a child, Alonzo watched the night his mother, a quiet woman who had always kept the house in order, come home from a day at the office only to find his father, a burly man who had never been physically gentle, on the kitchen floor. The father’s fists, the sudden splash of blood on the wooden floor, the shouts that echoed until dawn – Alonzo’s memory of that night was not a flashback but a living scene that he could almost smell. After the incident, his mother had taken him to a different house for a few weeks, but the sense of safety was forever fractured. Alonzo told me that, since that night, he could no longer look at a simple family gathering without the image of his father’s rage hovering in his mind. It was this early, visceral experience that set in motion a spiral of negative beliefs and fear that had lingered into his forties. The feeling that he had lost his capacity to feel joy – “I was once happy,” he told me – was not simply sadness; it was a belief that happiness was a luxury he could no longer afford. He also had lost his faith, not only in a higher power but in people. This loss of faith, according to Alonzo, made him feel as though the world was conspiring against him. The guilt that clung to him – that he had done nothing to stop the abuse – became a heavy weight that pulled his thoughts toward the image of the violence. These negative appraisals fed directly into his sense of threat. Because he believed the world was unsafe, he could not let himself relax, even if a trusted friend reassured him that he was safe. The feeling of untrustable safety, coupled with an internal belief that “I am doomed to be harmed again,” made the world a place where danger could erupt at any moment. That heightened sense of danger – the hypervigilance that kept his ears open to distant noises, the night vigilance that made him stare at the dark corners of his bedroom until the sunrise – compelled Alonzo to develop strategies to keep the threat at bay. He began to carry his camera, a tool he said would “catch the eyes of the devil if it should ever come.” He refused to be alone with anyone, even his partner, and when he was forced to work with a fellow farmer on a tractor, he would keep a close distance between them. He also kept himself physically occupied, always having a tool in hand, a task that made it easier to say “no” to conversations about anything that might bring up his trauma. This constant state of guarding left Alonzo exhausted and made him feel like he was living in a perpetual state of crisis. The more he relied on these maladaptive strategies, the more he felt isolated and trapped. Alonzo’s hypervigilance amplified his negative beliefs. Whenever he noticed a car horn or a sudden gust of wind, he would interpret it as a prelude to a violent event, reinforcing his belief that he could never be in a place that was truly safe. The sense of being unsafe was a relentless echo that kept the guilt about not intervening in his youth alive. Each time he imagined a scenario where he could have done more, he would freeze and find himself unable to breathe. The negative appraisals and threat perception were locked in a loop that made every day feel like a battle. When Alonzo’s strategies began to dictate the way he lived, the cycle tightened. He avoided any setting where he might be alone, even in his own home. He would bring his partner into the barn while he worked, but would still keep his feet on the floor of the field to feel the ground beneath him. By never letting himself be “alone with another person,” he was also avoiding the possibility of a conversation that might pull him back to the trauma. This avoidance prevented him from addressing the pain, which only made the negative appraisals – the sense that he had lost happiness, faith, and had inaction guilt – even more entrenched. He began to think that if he could not change the past, he might as well protect himself from any future harm by staying physically close to a person. The more he tried to suppress his thoughts, the more the mind filled with images of his father’s rage and his own longing for revenge, further feeding the threat perception. Now, during a routine check on his crops, Alonzo paused because his eyes caught a faint scar on a new seed bag – a reminder of the blood that had soaked the kitchen floor years before. The image flooded him with a wave of panic that he could not shake. He had long since stopped sharing these moments with his partner, preferring to stay in the field alone, yet even that solitude felt suffocating. He realized that his life had become a pattern of fear and avoidance that kept him from the small joys he had once taken for granted. The weight of the past, the sense that the world was a hostile place, and the crushing guilt of not having stopped the violence were all too heavy for him to bear alone. This realization pushed him to finally seek help, hoping that a therapist could guide him out of the loop and help him reclaim a sense of safety and meaning. Alonzo’s greatest fear remains that he will never feel at peace again, but he also holds a faint, stubborn hope that with support he might start to see the world as a place where he can truly belong.
